column15: We would like to see an improved understanding of the U.S. college application process, particularly regarding GPA conversions. column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
Modernize Teaching Methods
Encourage teachers to use more interactive and innovative approaches—project-based learning, digital tools, and real-world problem solving—so classes feel more relevant and engaging for today’s students.

Introduce More Oral Assessments
Incorporate oral exams and presentations to help students build confidence speaking up, think critically on their feet, and demonstrate their understanding without relying on AI tools.

Ongoing Teacher Development
Offer regular professional development focused on technology integration, diverse learning styles, and modern teaching strategies to ensure the learning experience stays dynamic and inspiring.

Holistic Evaluation
Move beyond exams and written assignments to include participation, collaboration, creativity, and self-reflection as part of student assessment.

Support for Well-Being and Character Growth
Continue promoting programs that build emotional intelligence, balance, and resilience—helping students thrive both academically and personally.

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15:
The school could focus on modernizing its teaching methods to better match how students learn today. Encouraging more interactive, discussion-based, and project-oriented learning, along with oral assessments, would help students build communication skills, creativity, and confidence.

It would also be valuable for the school to embrace AI as a learning ally rather than prohibit it, guiding students on how to use these tools responsibly for research, critical thinking, and creativity. Providing teachers with ongoing development on technology integration and effective AI use would help keep learning both engaging and relevant for the world our children are stepping into.

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15: De La Salle could improve by placing a stronger focus on student mental health and emotional well-being. Having more trained professionals and a safe, welcoming space where students can talk openly about their feelings would make a big difference. In addition, promoting more team-building activities and encouraging teachers to get to know their students on a personal level would help build trust and stronger relationships. This would not only support students in becoming better learners and better human beings but also allow teachers to recognize signs of bullying or other issues early on, so they can offer timely help and work together with families to provide the right support at home and at school. After, Del is their second home.

column15: There has to be an increased amount of communication between the various departments of the school even before decision are made.  Too often decisions are made without input or listening to those that will impacted by decisions.  While everyone understands that the admin, or board, IT, or facilities have ultimate responsibility and authority over various areas, a real community takes time to listen to each other before deciding on a plan of action, and maybe finding ways to mitigate the impact on the other groups. column15: A focus on the classroom experience.  While co-curriculars are important, and other events, too often it is the classroom experience that is sacrificed in the process.  Students miss too much class doing "other" things.  Planning and scheduling can eliminate about 80% of those issues.  Game days with shorter schedules, extended assemblies to deal with events and announcements...anything that allows for some consistency and uninterrupted class time.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
1) Streamline the IT programs and log-in’s for parents to access information. 4 separate portals is too many. 
2) Ensure a consistent use of Schoology across subjects for all teachers so class resources are centralized and easy to find for students from grade 7-12. (They are independent and capable enough to navigate computers, download materials, check messages to help them keep on top of their work, especially for those with lots of extracurriculars)
3) Improve system for booking PTI (online calendar would be great) and option for 10mins blocks, allow one day where interviews can begin at 3:30 or 4pm. This will be helpful for those living farther than a 5km radius from the school to make commute and school pick up easier. 
4) Have an archive of all DEL newsletters on the web portal accessible to all parents and students so that it is easier to look for information. Currently email communications can come from various school addresses, making sorting/searching a challenge. 
5) Ensure new teachers coming into DEL is well mentored and supported by experienced staff and also install a formal process to audit their classes in the beginning of the school year to ensure they are performing to the high standards expected of them.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: I personally think that the new schedule doesn’t provide what its original goal was: to mandate studying and to make sure students are productive during ALT/ free time. I think that the schedule does the opposite. Last year during my ILT I was much more productive and complete most of my homework during the day. Now since we have the same class every other day there is much more homework that is due in a shorter period of time, with less time to work on it. I also have been experiencing multiple tests or projects due on the same day, which makes it much harder to do well. Also sometimes the teacher use the ALT time to continue the lesson instead of letting us do work. This results in double the homework with no time to do it. This schedule has made me more stressed and made it harder to get my work done while being able to have a life and actually go to bed at a reasonable hour.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
We have noticed that the process of hiring new teachers may have had some challenges this year, based on the performance of a couple of them. In particular, the Grade 8 Science class and the Grade 11 Computer Science class seem to be experiencing issues based on conversations with our children.

In our opinion, for a school with the academic standards of De La Salle, it is important that new teachers understand the environment they are joining, specially since each subject builds the foundation for their post secondary life. This is especially important in Grade 11, where the courses they choose directly affect their university options, and in Grade 8, where core subjects like science are building the foundation for high-school success.

We fully understand that new teachers need time to adjust to the school’s expectations and academic culture. At the same time, timely support and course correction are important so students do not experience gaps or setbacks. You don't want a student to drop a subject not because they lack interest, but because the class is not engaging or the value is not coming through. We believe, students should feel motivated to attend and understand the value of the class, especially in subjects like Computer Science where strong instruction truly makes the difference. They need a teacher who can add real value, and this becomes even more evident when last year’s instructor (Mr. Caravaggio - DigiTech) set such a high standard. 

We also believe there would be value in gathering feedback from students. While younger students may be less objective or more influenced by excitement or frustration in the moment, feedback from students in the higher grades can offer meaningful insight into what is working well and where there may be challenges. This is especially relevant in a subject like Computer Science, where the difference from last year to this year has been noticeable.

We are thankful for what we have at Del and we're sharing this with the intention of supporting the school’s continued excellence and ensuring students receive the strong academic experience that De La Salle is known for and one of the reasons why we chose it.

Some students use the Alcorn Ave Field gate to enter the school due to Avenue Gate renovations. Recently, the gate is open at random intervals, requiring students to go around to Woodlawn or Farnham gates regardless (only teachers can unlock the Field gate).

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
1. I have two children (grade 10 and grade 12).  When my child in grade 10 gets an average <70% I get an email and immediately an action plan is in place. Where as for my grade 12 student, I raised the alarm early with my child's teacher about a course my child is experiencing difficulties and explained that the grades are required for university entrance, nothing was done.  I would understand if this was a public school system where getting a good teacher is a lottery but I'm PAYING tuition and this is not a public school system!!!! The selectiveness in teachers demonstrating concern/care for students' performance make me question the culture and environment Del promotes in its branding. I  have talked to numerous other parents and most tell the very same story.  I would like to think that Del is better than public school, that it offers more than just small class size and interesting extracurricular programs. 
Solution - do better by emphasize and mandating that all teachers need to provide the same level of care especially the senior grades as they depend on it for university application. 

2. I understand the new schedule was put in place to address the administration's concerns about kids being out of class/school property for extended time during school hours however, this schedule is not effective or helpful for all students - especially high school or grade 12s. There is no sufficient time for students to take a true mental health break or time to do homework.  Instruction time is too long, students lose concentration.  The 30 mins at the end of instruction time is not sufficient to cover all the kids that need support and ILT time is easily eaten up when my child has to compete for teacher tutorial. 
Solution - split the new schedule into two cohorts, junior school students need the supervision they should be under the new schedule. High school kids are more independent and need the extra time for homework, mental health break given their load. 

3. The school has a culture of favoring girls over boys. Their treatment of boys are unfairly harsh unlike the girls.  I remember Brother once wrote once to the teachers about creating an environment for boys at Del.  Why is this not taken seriously and or implemented? What message are you conveying to girls about equality? Is Del incorrectly forming these girls expectations and what happens when they get into the real world?  What message are you conveying to our young men?  How is this a Christian philosophy about equality and respect? 

4. Del has to audit the quality of its teachers.  My child's physics teacher does not teach the content, instead he hands out a "fact sheet and an exercise sheet" expecting the students to figure things out on their own.  My child is resorting to YOUTUBE to learn the material. Why am I paying tuition?????
Solution > regularly audit your teachers, 

5. Improve student life by giving students caring environment to learn and foster the environment of kindness, fairness and respect by having the TEACHERS demonstrate these values themselves. 

6. Why is there a "director or discipline" for minor infractions like uniforms? Shouldn't the focus be on implementing a safe environment for students?   How is a missing button harming any student?  I would rather see the funds used for other purposes...there should never be a police like presence at the school  if it is a safe environment.

column14: What do you like most about De La Salle College?
column15: The teachers were dedicated and provided exceptional academic and extracurricular activities. I liked that the size of my graduating class (<100 students) gave me opportunities to excel in many areas - academics, sports, music, drama. I also felt that the commitment to social responsibility and ethics grounded in the Catholic/Lasallian values resulted in compassionate graduates with a strong ability to think critically. I also felt lucky to use many of the facilities (i.e. music hall, field, arena) as I recognized that not all schools are able to offer these types of facilities. Finally, I think the "tough" academics prepared me well for university in terms of study habits and expectations of grades.

I'm not sure if this is applicable to the current situation at Del, but I'll nevertheless share a bit about my personal experience.

I attended Del from 1990 through 1994, in Grades 9 through 12, while Del was under the auspices of the then-named MSSB. I was a gifted student (i.e., identified as such by the MSSB in Grade 4), able to attain good grades in subjects of personal interest (mainly mathematics, sciences, some English courses, and all OAC courses) and passable grades in other subjects. I was engaged enough in classes, able to articulate thoughtful questions and relevant insights even when I held only a passing interest in the course. I'm sure I was regarded by most or all teachers as well-behaved and otherwise innocuous. Among students, I was generally shy and somewhat socially awkward.

I had intentionally self-limited my academic experience. I had never considered any extra-curricular activities at Del, nor was I ever approached or encouraged to consider them. I had also naively assumed that academic achievement as indicated solely by OAC grades were all that would be necessary to achieve success. There was only a single occasion when I was invited by John Hunt to attend a lunch and address at the Economic Club of Canada, but I had interpreted that as merely a reward for being a good student rather than an invitation to consider how I might engage the world. It would be years later that I would fully appreciate how a well-rounded education—going beyond what can be measured by grades—as well as personal investment in camaraderie and community, can have a significant impact on future success and fidelity to civic responsibilities.

I'm sharing my story because I wish that someone would have personally and directly invited me to participate in some of Del's extra-curricular activities. My own shyness and one-dimensional worldview of academic achievement were obstacles to curiosity and deeper engagement, making me deaf to announcements and general invitations. Perhaps what I now perceive as being overlooked was anomalous. In any case, I hope that Del now seeks to invite and encourage the full potential of each student at a personal level.

column15: The grace of Christ could be better exemplified.  A top button undone should not warrant punishment. column15: Transition time between schedules. I think that sometimes, 4 minutes isn't enough especially if you are going from one building to another because with this new schedule, a lot more people are moving to their new classrooms at the same time and so there is a lot of traffic. I think there should also be a longer transition time for homeroom to first period, because that is when every student is trying to go to a classroom and it can get very shuts and chaotic,

column14: Any additional comments about your experience or the College?
column15: Overall, my experience at De La Salle has been great and I felt like I learned so much academically and personally. I love the structure of the school because I really feel productive during the day as we don’t waste time and try to learn and work for as much of the class time we have as possible. I am extremely grateful for all teachers and staff for giving me the help and support I need, and I felt like I have made so much progress in my 2 years attending this school. The workload can get very overwhelming and stressful sometimes but the teachers are very understanding and flexible, which helps a lot. I have amazing memories at this school and I am so happy for this opportunity.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
I think that the new schedule needs to be scrapped and there needs to be a real emphasis on teaching students how to read/write/research without AI, which is easy for students to sneakily use. I think there needs to be measures to improve working conditions to reduce staff turnover (which the new schedule is largely responsible for). I think older teachers need to be brought in and valued more than they are now.

I also think that at times, the school stifles a diversity of views in a way that damages the mission. There is certainly a conservative lean that is emphasized. In the Politics course, the only partisan field trip was to see Stephen Harper speak. Through courses such as Philosophy, far-right sensationalists like Stephen Crowder were shown in class. I think there's a massive gap there... why not introduce students to the incredibly strong Catholic Socialist philosophical tradition, to show how Catholicism and progressive policies can interact? Why not discuss more progressive publications such as Pope Francis' Laudato Si? I had a Catholic prof (Prof. Boyagoda) that taught me about these thinkers in university, and I feel like leaving that out of the curriculum can make it a bit one-dimensional pedagogically (even if free discussion in class does occur). It's hard to truly promote Gospel values or critical thinking with the current format. Students need to know that Gospel values are not synonymous with conservatism if the mission of the school is to be fulfilled.

column14: What do you like most about De La Salle College?
column15:
Certainly the extra-curriculars; namely, Sports and the Debate Team. I had a sense that the emphasis and funding for these clubs decreased over my time (especially as the school tilted towards being more STEM focussed). I hope this has changed but fear it has not.

I also really liked the humanities teachers; many were very experienced and had a very positive impact on my life. Teachers like Mr. Calder, Mr. Iacobazzi, and Mr. Bellisario were absolutely fundamental in my development.

I also got to take advantage of several volunteer initiatives that helped me escape the biases of my socio-economic bubble. These opportunities should be expanded upon!

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15:
I outlined it pretty well in Question 13. But to summarize, I really appreciated and gained something from Del's "old school" teaching methods and schedule. However, I think there was a real lack of political and ideological perspectives presented to students (despite there being Catholic and progressive perspectives out there). 

I also feel like the school has become increasingly STEM focussed, so much so that as a Humanities student, I almost felt like I was making some sort of mistake not going into business. Maybe I'm biased, but I don't love that the school has gone so far in that direction.

I also think that teacher turnover really needs to be dealt with. Clearly, there's issues with working conditions and expectations.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: I understand the school is academically rigorous, but homework at the elementary level has been shown to have qualified benefits, and the sheer volume and frequency of it at Del often feels gratuitous. A de-emphasis on frequency and intensity of homework, specifically for the younger years would enable them to ramp up the homework to actually foster independent learning and work without inducing undue stress, and enabling them to maintain family connections, actually participate in extracurriculars without sacrificing academics, etc. It’s just a lot to ask in terms of work life balance for children in elementary, especially since the school has such a robust extracurricular and spirit life with many volunteering opportunities. It is a young age to begin to compromise on sleep to get everything done.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: Parent-Teacher interviews need to be longer. I am looking forward to the new building being completely accessible. I am hoping the main building (auditorium/gym) could somehow be renovated to be accessible. Students in Grade 7-8 (with foundation set in lower grades) probably need more guidance on anti-bullying and not being peer pressured. There seems to be some rough-housing among boys at recess/changing for gym that needs more teacher supervision. I believe there are still racist "jokes"/comments being made that are not caught by teachers. The school is predominantly white so students from other ethnicities may need extra supports to ensure inclusion. All students need to know there is zero-tolerance of bigotry/stereotypes/racism. Teachers need to stay alert with students trying to use phones/bending rules etc. There is still some stigma/hesitation among students to access student services/mental health resources. Need to normalize it as much as physical health. Probably need to build out the library/research/resource centre and ensure students know the importance of researching assignments etc. - both with books (especially for Grades 5-8) and online.

column14: What do you like most about De La Salle College?
column15: Adherence to no phones allowed. Adherence to uniform requirements. Teachers are caring and hard working. Have known several teachers that have been especially supportive. Trips and retreats that allow for student bonding. Parent community is extremely generous and creative in supporting the school and students. Special events that bring parents onto the campus. Special events for the students (Spirit Day, ShareLife Day). Discipline and routine of assigning homework, tests, quizzes, assignments - with teacher follow up and notification to parents if issues. Connection between school and parents. Coaches for sports and extracurricular club staff leaders. Focus on music, drama, art - essential for developing whole student, and artistic endeavours aid academic success.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: The college did not embrace diversity of thought or teach its students to think critically about Catholic principles and how they apply in the real world. To fully love all people, as Jesus did, the school should create a safe space for diversity including intellectual, religious, sexual orientation, learning styles etc. I did not feel safe to bring my authentic self to school due to fear. I saw pervasive bullying by the administrations "favourites" that was unchecked because those male students met the hyper-masculine, Italian-Catholic mold.

column15:
Teach how to critically think about the Catholic faith to better prepare the students. For example - discuss the history of child abuse in the Church. I was unprepared to be Catholic in the world we live in today. 
Support all personal development experiences, even if they don't align with Catholic teachings. This will demonstrate how to truly love and accept your brothers and sisters. Example - one of my core memories from De La Salle was a boy in the grade above me being told that he was not allowed to bring his boyfriend to prom. This deeply affected me and taught me that people who are different should hide their authentic self and be ashamed if it does not subscribe to the beliefs of the system.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: I attended Del when it operated according to Day 1/Day 2 schedule, and that worked really well for me. I learned recently that the school has moved away from this scheduling and I didn't find the new scheduling appealing; ending the day before 3 pm made it easier for commuting, but I also think that extending the day close to (or beyond) 4 pm makes for a very long day for students. I like the idea of adding more breaks and flexibility into students' schedules, but I also think the College must be mindful of family time at home (long days at school can prevent that), and that some students may find the day too long (I know I would have). Allowing time away from school to recharge is also important.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
The schools only physics teacher, Mr. Rieger is a bad teacher, and every other student I’ve spoken to (including very academically driven students) feels completely lost in his lessons. He doesn’t teach well, he never goes over examples in class, often concepts we haven’t learned in class are on examinations, and his lessons are very unengaging. All of these are especially bad, since grade 11 and 12 science is vital, and there’s no other teacher who you can ask physics questions to.

As well, the student services are not helpful. At other schools, students have a specific guidance counsellor who would check in with their assigned students and who guide said students with anything they need. At Del, it’s hard to book an appointment, and if you do, the walls are paper thin so anything you want to say can be heard by anyone in the Main Office, so if students want to talk about something personal, it’s very uncomfortable. This is however, compensated by how wonderful, supportive and open to conversation almost all the teachers are.

I’ve also noticed that a lot of students don’t like Del. I don’t know if that’s just a feature of teenagers, but I think it’s sad how many students don’t actually enjoy Del. Maybe more fun days like out of uniform days and holiday celebration could help students feel happier here? 

Also the black chairs in the innovation centre are pretty painful to sit in for long periods of time.

column15:
Most all of the teachers are wonderful, and make me feel very motivated to learn. Almost every teacher I’ve had is super passionate about what they teach, and is open to answering questions and talking with students outside of class time to help elaborate on course content and expanding on topics outside of the course. The teachers are definitely the highlight of Del.

I also like how pushed we are, and how Del prepares students for university (which is why I joined).

Controversial opinion, but I like the dumb rules, and the pseudo-bureaucracy that Del is because it’ll prepare me to deal with dumb things and systems as an adult.

The campus is also gorgeous (especially the Great Lawn and Heritage House).

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
More regularity and consistency with junior school afternoon courses, the 8 day roll makes tests and frequency with students hard. I think it is also very confusing for students. 

I believe some elements of the new schedule are positive because they provide structure for high school students. However, many students express how stressed they are with the same amount of work and less “free time” to complete it. Tutorials are very inconsistent for high school students, teachers are only available 1-2 times every 8 day cycle. 

Teacher schedules are still very inconsistent amongst staff, some teachers are teaching over hours while others are under and receive many on-calls. Some teachers are teaching too many students. How does one maintain communication with all those parents? 

It’s hard to connect with departments. The department meetings were very helpful and a good weekly check points, I believe it created stronger communication and better community. 

Many teachers have no where to lay their head. Many staff, including myself are carrying multiple bags or storing stuff in random places at the school. Every department should have an office or space with a desk. Everyone is a nomad  

The technology issues in the school are very disruptive, especially the computers and auditorium equipment, perhaps more people working in the IT department?

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
1) Find Catholic staff and leaders who are passionate about sharing the faith, can connect with the students, and focus on fixing their practice rather than 'fixing' their students. Most of the Catholic leaders in my graduating year were quite disconnected from the student body. Very little took them seriously.

2) Better yet, find higher-quality staff and train them better. Pick the prospects that have drive and passion. And I won't sugarcoat it - pay them more. Make it clear to your teachers that they need to integrate themselves into the community and passionately dedicate time to the College (extracurriculars, office hours and tutorials, etc.). Make your current staff like your school so they put a good word in for future staff. There is no excuse for not doing this.

Your teachers should do more than impart knowledge. They also need to be role models, collaborative with their fellow staff, and collaborative with their students. This is what I mean by "higher quality." My graduating year did not have these people.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
The deterioration of the music department was one of the most regrettable memories of my grade 12 year. The main issue was the conversion of the Music Hall into a lunch area, which led to music classes being held in the auditorium. This caused a lot of class time to be wasted setting up the stage and cleaning up the stage. Additionallly, the music instructors did not have the expertise of previous instructors, Larry Shields and Craig Thompson. For example, I played Skyfall by Adele in my grade 8 music class, and then Ms. DiNardo made us play it again in grade 12. She did not believe any of us when we said we had already performed this very easy song five years prior.

Additionally, the conversion of the arena was unwanted by most of the student body, and it would have been beneficial to consult the students on whether this construction was even necessary.

Lastly, the ability to switch tutorial sections was made forbidden in my grade 12 year, which was a massive disappointment many students, including myself. Please make this possible again.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: Relax restrictions on areas for approved student food and beverage consumption. Presumably, the College is aware of the gruelling length of Canadian winters, and should also be aware that said winters yield unsavoury temperatures outdoors. This relegates students to only one room on the first floor of the main building, the cafeteria, for all eating drinking and general student recreation. It seems unusual for the school to have spaces, that seem otherwise tenable as a place for students to sit about, discuss, and feed themselves, sitting empty and lifeless without purpose. One might be familiar, for example, with a 'C-shaped' couch set that sits by the Eastern doors of the Innovation Centre, which faces out to a quaint display of lush greenery and flora. For unclear reasons, said couch set, along with its dedicated dining table, are forbidden to even have the implicated presence of foods in sight. Oftentimes, there might even be a teacher who will expel all the students in the general vicinity of this couch set for "not being somewhere else". As a result, one can on occasion find wrappings of foodstuffs that have been quickly shoved into the crevices of the seating to avoid detection. Perhaps if one were to permit some consumption and congregation in spaces where they seem otherwise appropriate, there may be less frequency of waste left undisposed.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: Communication to parents, especially first your parents could be better. During our first year at the college, it was at times difficult to understand how to prepare and what to prepare for for the various events and initiatives that were coming up. The best example is the first day of school. The communications leading up to the first day of school included opportunities to be greeted at the front doors and escorted around the school, including the assignment of a mentor. Our experience was that this did not happen. My child followed other students who were returning to the school and walked into the closest doors that happened to be at the back of the school. There was no welcome committee as promised. During the entire first year, there was no mentor that was ever assigned. So this is one example of the school not following through with some of its stated commitments. All that said our experience generally at the school once we were acclimated has been very very positive.

column14: Any additional comments about your experience or the College?
column15: At several Parent Association meetings recently, one parent ( reading from a prepared statement ) has insisted on setting up a snitch line for kids that may be the apparent victims of racism or bullying. We are not opposed to having an avenue for kids to come forward comfortably to raise concerns like these, but this whole thing to us sounds like something out of the diversity, equity and inclusion playbook. Which in our view is not a good thing. The parent has talked about the existence of hate and violence at the school. Which to be honest is news to us. Also, It’s not entirely clear what the communication tool will be for kids to lodge complaints, who will assess the complaints, and who will decide on their validity and any consequences for the apparent perpetrators. This whole thing worries us greatly because this is one of the reasons that we came to Del LaSalle, to avoid such complications that may exist in the public school system. We believe in the promotion of tolerance through the teachings of the Bible, not through some vague goals of fighting so called hate, which by the way, is an emotion and it’s not clear to us at all how one would regulate an emotion in teenagers. In any event, we hope to find out more about this and to have the opportunity to raise concerns if we feel it is not structured appropriately.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: The course workload of the junior school can often be overwhelming for the kids particularly when they have multiple tests and assignments in a day/week.  While we understand the need to continuously test the kids, an observation would be that the teachers can do a better job at scheduling the assignments and tests so they don't continuously overlap with other classes.  Perhaps an electronic calendar for each class would help in planning tests and assignments so that teachers can observe the workload of the students on a day to day basis.  Further, we believe there is room to lighten the work load and still maintain the excellent academic standing of the school.  There appears to be quite the difference in workload at Del vs other high ranking private schools.  Perhaps this is done by design, but the kid's extracurricular activities after school (hockey, dance, etc) become virtually impossible to maintain with the workload that exists.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: Some suggestions that I believe would help De La Salle College improve include: opening the music hall back up while the new building isn’t ready. Now that it’s getting colder, there isn’t enough space in the caf for grade 9s, 10s, some grade 11s and 12s on break, and the 10/20 minute overlap with junior school. Also, more break is fundamental in the learning of students. Having to sit in a class for 100 minutes straight (where some teachers teach the whole time) is draining, and most students zone out and cannot take in that much information at once. Even physically, having to sit in a chair for 100 minutes straight is painful and can even cause physical issues. As a grade 10 student, I find myself spending hours in class, with only a 40 minute break (where much of it gets cut down due to going to my locker or buying a lunch), simply to go home and do hours of homework non stop. I also feel like this schedule and removing the music hall has distanced people. Overall, I genuinely feel drained and I feel as though it is too much for an anyone, let alone a teenager.

column15: Once students graduate from high school, life changes. Yes, you prep them for college or university studies. That is the easy part. The hard part is adjusting to college life. The same can be said for beyond university studies and into careers and life. It would be good if someone could talk with them about what to expect from life. It shouldn't be teachers or their parents but someone who might have a more diverse view and experience. This isn't about marks because there are no right or wrong answers. It is not about advice. It is about showing them a different perspective on what may or may not happen in their lives, or what they might experience.

column15: One suggestion I would have for De La Salle would be to adjust the schedule slightly to factor in the time it takes for students to transition from period-to-period. As it stands, teachers allow students to leave five minutes before the period ends to do so, but there are times where a teacher may forget and as result, the students end up late for their next class. To address this, I suggest ending the class three-to-five minutes earlier on the schedule, and name the new, short block of time as 'transition time' or something of that insinuation.

column15: Since it is the first year where we kickstarted the new 4 day schedule, there are many improvements and feedback that should be taken into consideration. There is no time to do actual work within breaks, leaving students to complete work after school. Some schedules were also not balanced nicely, giving students with four classes one day, and only one class the next day. This schedule overall burns the students out quickly, and as a grade 12 who has already been comfortable with the workload, this year has been especially difficult. I wish there was more time in the schedule to complete work. This also relates back to the grade 9’s, where they have so many classes in one day, with only a minimal time for lunch and break.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: More awareness of what’s really happening with students. This survey is a step towards that, I guess. But the hateful words that people regularly use here that no one in admin notices is a bit appalling! And also all the mental illness and challenges everywhere is disheartening. I received a lot of help with my mental illness, but other people are either afraid to speak up or have done so and are receiving inadequate help. I know some people who are feeling judged for the support that they need to receive. And there’s more I would like to say, but I honestly don’t know what to say. I’ve appreciated my experience here. I would say also though that I am glad to leave. Some people I will miss, and some experiences. But I also have a lot of difficult memories here. Please make adjustments to listen better to students regularly.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: I think shortening the periods to one hour instead of 70 minutes would be slightly better, as the 70 minute classes can be quite long at sometimes and my productivity has slipped in those last 10 minutes. 60 minutes would allow, I think, for better productivity and engagement in class without it going on for too long. The thirty minute ILT time blocks are nice, but it would be nice if they were slightly longer to allow a bit more work to be done. Also, there are nowhere near enough Math and Science Office Hours, which is not ideal as these are the subjects people often need the most assistance with, and it would be nice to have more of that compared to the Writing Centre, which is often empty. Additionally, the 8-day schedule is very confusing for us high school students because we don't know where our teachers will be and when because it constantly switches. Going back to a four-day schedule would be way less confusing, I believe, for students and teachers alike. This may be my own opinion, but I believe the choir at Mass actually takes away from the spirit of the Mass itself, and it feels more like a show/performance than an act of Catholic worship. It also would be nice to have some more field trips provided other than the retreat (i.e. Toronto Islands, day trip to Niagara etc.). It would be nice to have more opportunities throughout the year to see our marks to know where we have to improve throughout the year

column14: What do you like most about De La Salle College?
column15: Del's community is the best part of the school. I love how united we are: parents, students, staff, and admin, and how everybody always supports eachother and cares for one another. We are all an adopted family and Del feels like a second home. The facilities are great this year (and I really appreciate the addition of the Music Hall back to the music department), and I particularly appreciate the Writing Centre as a quiet workspace. The staff, particularly this year, are exceptionally good at what they do and very supportive and kind. I have not been this pleased with my teachers in many years. I do appreciate being finished at 12:45 on some days as well, so I can go home, do homework, and rest.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
Guidance should put a bigger emphasis in gr9-10 on maintaining good grades rather than pushing the gr12 grades are the only ones that matter because they DO matter if you want to apply to the states and some abroad programs additionally schools like McGill look at gr11 and 12 marks and marks ONLY (no other additional essays or résumé’s etc) so it’s important for students to realise how it effects their futures clearer. 

ALSO: Please please please open up power school so we can see our marks because with the weighting it’s hard to fully place how we’re doing so only seeing it a few times a year is a lot more stressful then always being able to see it because it blindsides us. We’d all rather know how we’re doing so this way we’re realistic with the amount of work and effort we need to continue to put in. It’s easy to think you’re doing okay in a course and then get the marks back and it’s much worse or vice versa, thinking you’re doing badly and stressing just to realise you’re doing fine.

column15: I think that the schedule does not provide enough breaks for those taking a full course load (8 classes). I also think that the caf food is EXTREMELY overpriced, and there are minimal options. The pizza is greasy and not made from real dough, the pasta is soggy, and there are no healthy, yummy, and diverse options! $3 for a cookie is a ridiculous price, and I will be boycotting the caf. The arts and academic clubs are criminally underfunded and are not put in the spotlight at Del. There is one grade 12 in the music class which is sad.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: PLEASE GIVE US MORE STUDENT COMMON AREAS. The caf is not enough space, it is often full and overwhelming, and we cannot eat in the research center. With winter coming up the caf becomes more unbearably full everyday. PLEASE CHANGE THE SCHEDULE. I have experienced 4 different schedules in my time here and this is by far the worst one. Students with 8 classes are struggling. There is no breaks for them and no opportunities for office hours that don't fall into lunch which is their only break all day, meaning students are suffering academically. Classes being an hour and forty minutes is absurd and just tires everyone out. I personally do not feel the brunt of the impacts of this schedule as I am in grade 12 and have less classes, but my sister is in grade 10 with a full class load and I see how this schedule has negatively affected both her grades and her mental health. Also, the caf prices have inflated at an alarming speed so please lower the insanely expensive prices. In conclusion, please give us more student common areas where we can eat, and fix the schedule.

I used to love the math, science, and English offices but now due to the new schedule they are barely usable. I used to love the upstairs music hall as a common area but now that is gone. column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: Creating a equal and encouraging environment for BOTH men and women. Celebrating BOTH men and women's achievements. Sports included. If one male team is offered letterman jackets for their win, the same should be done for the women's team. To eliminate any kind of unnecessary fear mongering that is associated with the catholic faith. I think some teachers forgot that they were speaking to CHILDREN. Each child comes from a unique background and is a unique individual. Anti-LGBTQ rhetoric or judgement could be a very harmful or scary for a child who is just trying to figure themselves out. The intense labelling of things as "bad" or "evil" can also be pretty damaging.  I hope the school is doing a better job of celebrating the wins/success of students that isn't just STEM related. Unfortunately it was not until I had a teacher in the 11/12 grade who acknowledged and celebrated my strengths in the humanities that I actually considered myself an intelligent person. Del really did not foster an environment that grew or uplifted my confidence as a young woman- at all. Lastly Joy! while I found joy in-between classes with friends or in class with certain amazing teachers, or while on a sports team- the school really didn't foster a lot of joy. It didn't feel like an overly happy place. Again, I really hope all of this has changed.

column15: The people, the friends I made. While Del did force me to grow up very quickly- it was kind of like I was "in it" or "surviving it" with my peers. It bonded us in a very special way and I am grateful for that community.

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15: I think Del administration could really lead with a lot more empathy, understanding and compassion for their students. Not every child has the same skills, or ways of learning. Just because a child is struggling with math or science, fear mongering and putting them on "academic probation" is not going to instill confidence to make them try and work harder at the subject. If anything its going to confirm what they always believed - that they are not good at math and science. It wasn't until I began working and got to reapproach the way I learn,  learning from a place of openness and confidence that I realized I am not actually bad at this!

column15: I attended the College with the hope of a strong education from a Catholic institution that would instil Catholic values. Your school is ultimately an embarrassment and hardly representative of the Catholic values I want my children to bring into the world. Your awareness of and support for students’ needs is laughable. All my female friends report that the President of the school does not even make eye contact with female students. The last thing I want is my daughter to feel like the actual President of her own school does not believe in her success. The College has created deep and long lasting scars for myself and most others I know. Anyone who does not meet the mould of an ideal Lasallian image, no matter their commitment to service, education, or Christianity, is treated less than human. I, and many others quite frankly, would happily see this school shut down, defunded, and paying out large sums to the countless teenagers they’ve lead to mental health extremes. Don’t forget, you’ve created hundreds of well-educated and soon to be politically/legally powerful graduates. It would be a shame if they used that power to rightfully remove yours.

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15:
I feel that the new schedule requires some improvement. Although I understand the reason for removing the flex-mod schedule, I do not think the new schedule is a good replacement. I feel that the length of classes is much too long for someone to properly concentrate, especially since teachers have the ability to keep us in for an extra 30 minutes. I feel that there are certain classes that require this amount of time, such as music, or a content-heavy course like biology, but for other classes, such as math, there isn't really a need to stay there for 100 minutes, especially if most people lose concentration by the half-way point and aren't properly engaged for the rest of the class. 

For both grade 9 and grade 10, I was able to properly handle taking 8 courses, two of which were reach-ahead in both years, and 2 AP exams in grade 10. The long breaks I was able to have during the school week, even with taking that many courses, was definitely the biggest contributor to my success. I initially started the school year also taking 8 courses, but found that in that case, everyday I had only 20 minutes in the morning for break, and 40 minutes for lunch. This is not a lot of time, especially considering that eating lunch takes up a good portion of my longest break, and that I feel that it's reasonable to want to spend a break, or at least part of it, socializing with my friends after having 3 very long classes. As someone who also takes extracurriculars, the schedule is extremely unhelpful. Since dropping a course, I now have one 70 minute break every one or two days a week, but I definitely had more time to complete my work at school last year and the year before even though I was taking one more course than I am now. 

Additionally, I'm not sure if there's a certain reason for the 8 day schedule, but as a student, the 8-day schedule is more confusing than anything else. A 2-day schedule, or even a 4-day schedule, would make much more sense considering we alternate between the same 4 classes every other day. More often than not, I don't know what "day" it is, only that I have half of my classes on one day, and the rest on the other. Since every day was distinct last year, it was very easy knowing what "day" corresponded with the classes that I had. This schedule also makes it much more difficult to attend office hours, as my breaks are not long enough for me to effectively get any help, and that the 8-day schedule makes it confusing to figure out which days of the week, and at what time, have running office hours, as every other day feels the exact same despite the "day" being different.  

I really wish this change didn't come right during one of the two most important years of high school. The lengths of my breaks getting shorter, and the frequency at which I have them also decreasing, while my workload increases in amount and difficulty, is extremely unhelpful. I understand the reason behind this change in class length, and the requirements the school is required to fulfill, but I believe there must be a better alternative to the schedule we have now.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: I know a lot of Del policies are meant to prepare us for the real world and university, and I think there are many benefits to being strict about things like uniform, phones, etc, but I also believe that at some point it becomes genuinely stifling. Things like only wearing sprit wear for casual days and getting a slip if you so much as wear a sweater over it, only allowing black shoes for walking to and from school, getting slips for loitering even if we’re not necessarily being loud- these are small restrictions but there are many, they make up our day to day student life, and it accumulates. In the same vein, I’m on the creative arts committee, and we’ve been having trouble getting an instagram account dedicated to the arts. We’re a group of passionate kids wanting to promote the arts in our school and it feels like even small things like this have huge obstacles to overcome because of the “anti-fun” attitude of the school, for lack of better word. Obviously the point of an educational institution is education, but for a school that prides itself in its community (and it should), we don’t always feel like the community exists outside of academics.

column14: Any additional comments about your experience or the College?
column15: It’s great that student services is so available and most of the time they are helpful, but it’s also been my (and my friends)’s experience that they don’t always help if you’re feeling overwhelmed. It’s sort of an inside joke between us that if we’re upset, overwhelmed, or stressed, we need to just “wait for the break” and it’ll sort itself out, because that’s the common response we get when we talk about these feelings to our guidance counsellors- no matter what time of year it is, it’s just “that time of year” and whatever break or long weekend is closest will help. This year in particular has felt harder than the rest (maybe just since its grade 12), and this mindset stresses me out if anything. I’m managing alright now, but I worry that if I need more help later, I won’t find it.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
- The school environment feels overly strict and militaristic. Children need more time to simply be kids—learning should be fun and engaging, not harsh or rigid.
- Please bring back the Community Program for younger grades. It was offered in Grade 7 but is missing in Grade 8.
- Increase the number of school trips that offer hands-on learning experiences. One-day retreats to churches aren't that enriching and not fun. Consider outings to the theatre, sports games, museums, or even simply skating at Ramsden Park. There are so many good and local options with living in the city!
- Extend lunch periods to give students more time to socialize and decompress.
- Incorporate more dress-down days, pep rallies, and sports days to help students feel connected to the school community.
- Encourage families to attend school sports events so it create a sense of community and school spirit - let them wear Del Clothing and be proud (e.g., homecoming).
- Organize community service events like volunteering at the Daily Bread Food Bank. Don’t just talk about volunteerism, show students how to participate meaningfully.
- Refresh and update the after-school clubs to make them more engaging and relevant to student current interests.
- Introduce a warm-weather uniform option, even simply a golf shirt. All other schools do this and kids would be proud to wear them. 
- Plan an overnight and fun Grade 8 graduation trip to help students bond and celebrate their achievements.
-Allow students to participate in dances with other private schools. De La Salle is currently the only one not involved -let them interact with kids in other schools - it's important. 
- During exam periods, organize active/wellness activities to teach students the importance of movement and stress management (mental and physical health are so important!). Organize mandatory games or physical activities in school (gym/field etc) during the exam periods in the afternoons after the exams - before heading home to study. This models healthy habits they’ll need in University.  Start some new traditions around this).  
- Celebrate the end of exams with something fun for the students - it’s a great way to reward their hard work. again -something they will need to do in University but can be done in fun ways.  Let the kids organize it!

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15:
1. Focus more on the whole child, not just academic performance.  Report cards only show percentage grades, but what about other important skills like organization, collaboration, responsibility, initiative, and independence? How are students doing socially? How are they managing stress? How do they interact with peers? These are critical indicators of development and should be included.
2. Implement an electronic system for booking parent-teacher interviews. The current process is outdated and unnecessarily difficult. It gives the impression that teachers don’t want to meet with parents. Even public schools use simple online systems - this should be an easy fix.
3. Let them have some dress down days and give them a summer uniform - they're kids!

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: Del's culture creates a false equivalency between academic rigour and marks.  Teachers are expected to give low marks as a way of affirming academic rigour.  This harms children's confidence while also hobbling them for university admissions against public schools where grades are higher.  Del needs a fundamental cultural reorientation where it reaffirms academic rigour while setting children up for success for university admissions.

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15: University Planning:  1. Del would benefit from acknowledging that universities weight grade 11 marks more heavily, especially for early admissions, and recognize its marking scheme in grade 11 disadvantages kids in university admissions, as a result. 2. The school would benefit from investing more in guidance staff to proactively plan for student's university admissions. Our experience with our daughter at Greenwood was much different.  (Example: my grade 11 child is in grade 12 business and guidance knows he is interested in university business programs.  He was denied the opportunity to join DECA in grade 11.  Why?  Because the school put students in charge for determining who would be admitted to DECA.  DECA is competitive.  So, students were set up to select their own competition.  This would never happen in school sports tryouts.  It's unethical.  The school would benefit from bringing in an speaker on ethics in business which the teachers who made that decision should also attend.  The guidance counselor spoke to the DECA teacher lead and nothing happened.  So, my child has lost the opportunity to put DECA in grade 11 on his university admissions and to have the enriching experience.  3. The school needs to stop trying to prevent students from writing AP exams.  Some teachers recommend who can write it or not.  Why?  To protect the school's ranking with the College Board?  The school promotes itself as offering AP exams.  Please stop trying to prevent children from writing them.  The DECA incident and AP approach are culturally linked.  Both represent the school denying children the opportunity to succeed.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15: Regarding the schedule, i feel it doesn’t help complete my work and manage my workload. I am in class all day and have only 35 minutes where i am not in class. Comparing this to elementary school, i have even less time to eat, play and interact with friends. I feel high school should be a part of life where students learn independence through multiple breaks during the day. As well, I am not able to attend office hours during my break this year. Going to a lunch tutorial guarantees not being able to eat at all during the day as my lunch break is my only break. I then need to attend tutorials after school, a time which i am not always available. With regards to ALT, I feel i am not able to get much of my work done as it takes me a bit of time to understand the new lesson we would’ve learned in class. When I get home, I often feel very tired after a long day of sitting in class and then find myself overwhelmed with large amounts of homework. I participate in extra curricular activities after school and unfortunately sometimes have to miss them to complete my school work. I feel that my life at school has taken over much of my time outside of school.

column15: During my lunch period, i often find it difficult to find a place to eat lunch. The only places to eat lunch are in the cafeteria or outside. However, when it rains the cafeteria is the only option. With only 1 place for the entire school to eat lunch, the cafeteria becomes very chaotic with the junior school moving in and out, the line to buy food being very long and the limited seats to sit at to eat lunch. At the beginning of the year, me and a few friends would eat in the com-tech room as allowed by the teacher. It was a very quiet place to eat lunch and work on any homework we may have had. Recently, our eating privileges have changed and we are no longer able to eat lunch there. Winter is right around the corner and with the cafeteria being the only place to eat our lunch, I feel it is going to become very chaotic and i might find myself having to go the entire day without eating due to its limited space.

column15: When I attended I had free education up until Gr. 10, then paid after that. (Eventually Catholic school boards achieved full funding.) It was struggle for me to pay, but I managed it with part time jobs, summer jobs, etc. I sometimes fear that nowadays, with Del being private, the tuition is so high that someone in a position similar to what my life was like as a teenager, would not be able to manage the tuition, and would be unable to come. I know you have bursaries. I pray that you are doing everything in your power to expand the availability of bursaries, so that even young people from modest income families, can still choose to attend Del. It's a wonderful place.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
There seem to be several inefficiencies that are affecting staff productivity and overall morale. The IT department’s response time to emails and technical issues is often quite delayed, which makes it difficult to address important matters promptly. It may be worth considering whether they need additional support or staffing to help improve efficiency.

Parking continues to be a major challenge, with teachers experiencing daily stress trying to find a spot in the morning. This creates unnecessary frustration at the start of the day.

There is also a lack of adequate workspace for teachers. Some departments have offices while others are limited to lockers or shared areas, making it difficult to stay organized and complete work efficiently. Every teacher should ideally have access to a functional workspace to perform their duties effectively.

Additionally, some departmental structures could be reviewed to ensure consistency and fairness. For instance, it’s unclear why there are two art department heads. The current format of morning meetings may also not be the best use of time. Returning to regular department meetings could help improve communication, collaboration, and support—especially for new teachers who benefit from weekly interaction with their colleagues.

The new schedule this year has created unnecessary rigor and stress for students. Not all teachers are using the additional time in the same way, and students are receiving the same amount of work but with less time to complete it. From my conversations with them, many students seem unhappy with the change.

The junior school afternoon rotations also appear to be quite disorganized. Teachers who teach multiple junior classes are constantly moving between rooms and see their classes inconsistently. The 8-day rotation adds to the irregularity and makes it difficult to establish routine and continuity in learning.

column15:
Communication in the beginning of our first year was excellent then went downwards. Must address the communication with parents. 

I hope that we can have some consistency when marking our kids work. I am shocked to see the differences between the teachers marking skills. It seems unfair that a child would have better grades if they are with a different teacher or vice versa. 

I also believe that there should be a bit more time in class for junior school to work on homework with the teacher present for help. Once a child attends tutorials it leaves little time in the evening for family with homework.

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15: There should be more investment in professional development for the newer faculty, especially around rapport with students, and maintaining professionalism and confidentiality. At times, comments made in class about other teachers, or school decisions (i.e. new schedule) can unintentionally create an environment where students feel staff are against the school. In addition, teachers should avoid discussing individual students with other students to maintain trust and confidentiality. *this particularly applies to newer faculty* All in all, it's important that classroom dialogue remains respectful and supportive to foster a more positive and united environment. Newer staff needs to be reminded that words matter and the way teachers communicate, even casually, can have a lasting impact on how students perceive themselves and the school community. Language that is dismissive or sarcastic can undermine the supportive culture that the school is known for.

Their experience at the college was positive and their teachers were consistently dedicated, professional, and supportive. We continue to value the strong academic foundation and community that the college provides. However, we have noticed a shift with some of the newer faculty, where the same level of professionalism is not always present. We hope to see renewed consistency in maintaining standards that have defined the school's reputation for excellence.

My son this year tried to attend another teacher’s tutorial afterschool because it worked better with his schedule and he was turned away. We are trying to foster good learners and we want to give them flexibility and opportunity. column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
Handling of serious misbehaviour- At times there is a disappointing contrast between the strict enforcement of rules regarding uniforms, lateness and home work and the muddled handling of more serious behaviour problems, like bullying and unhinged antics in the boys locker room last year ( among grade 6 boys). This year in grade 7, we have heard of the same boys causing their science teacher to break down in tears and spraying another boy in the face with bug repellent during the class trip to OPC. We also heard of a current student who was badly beaten up by other students on Founder’s Day a few years ago and the culprits are still at the school. Why aren’t these more serious infractions addressed clearly and definitively?

Better retention of key staff - We were disappointed to learn that Ms Di Nardo, the energetic and talented head of music, left after last year. She has not been replaced as far as we know. Her departure seems to highlight a fairly common turnover of staff from year to year. Does the administration do performance reviews ? Exit interviews ? What can be learned from these departures to ensure better recruitment and retention ?

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15:
Besides a more consistent and effective handling of serious behaviourial problems among a few students and better retention of key teaching staff, as noted above, I think Del needs a more effective governance. 

In the particular, the different roles and responsibilities of the President and the Principal seem unclear and overlapping. While I understand that the President has broad responsibilities, I suspect that over time many of these responsibilities have been practically assumed by the Principal. For example, I was surprised to hear that the President is in charge of Human Resources. Does the President actively manage HR in its fullest sense, like in a well run business ? If it, who is actually running HR ? It must be a crucial function as it would be in any school.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
Consider varying days of week some clubs operate on. Sometimes students cannot participate in certain activities due to scheduling conflicts between certain clubs. 
ALT time seems to have become extensions of the subject matters class time. Strongly suggest where possible that this time, while supervised becomes more independent to allow students to develop their self-discipline skills and also work on subject matter that they need to most focus on. If structured this way can also allow for one -or-one or small group follow-up with subject teacher in room. 
My children are self-motivated and academically advanced... despite all of the talk of Del homework being overwhelming - they frequently finish all work during the day and have limited/no homework to complete at home. Please consider how your most advanced students can be engaged in subject material and pushed to the next level. Often subject matter is a repeat of past year... or is too focused on learning knowledge/facts - which can be sourced electronically. Key skill for future is independent/critical thinking and is this truly being nurtured and developed as much as it could? Tailoring program in this direction will truly set Del La Salle apart from all other schools. 
Ensure students are aware of available spaces for independent study and group work after school. Cafeteria space is not sufficient/adequate. Please make additional spaces available for students who depart Del at later times and encourage students to stay back after school to complete work/participate in activities/build friendships.

column14: Please share any suggestions that would help De La Salle College improve.
column15:
DLS needs to do a better job of addressing the mental well-being of all students. Having a speaker once or twice a year is not sufficient grounds for mental health support. The school fails to recognize the challenges students face at all levels, whether they are academic high achievers or not. Both groups face unique mental health challenges towards happiness and well-being, one of which is marks.
The school needs to stop messaging that “marks don’t matter” and not wanting students and parents to focus on marks when so much of what Del does is mark-based. Entry to the school is based on marks, Prize night recognizes students based on marks, students are put on Academic Probation if their marks aren’t a certain minimum, and students are put on ALT if their marks aren’t a certain minimum. A large part of university acceptance is also based on marks.
So, rightly or wrongly, marks do matter, and many parents and students want to see their school marks on Schoology on an ongoing basis so they can assess and understand where they are at and what can be done to support the child if needed. Having had several conversations with parents at other private schools, I’ve noticed that no one approaches mark visibility like DLS does. 
I would like to see Del be more transparent about where the cohort averages are on the subject, not just in class. Del surely won’t share what percentage of students are above 80%, but I would hope they are looking at the cohort as a whole and assessing if a large share of students are failing or below 65%. Considering the ramifications on mental health of those students not having access to their marks until November, it’s important to know if a significant portion of students are struggling. Having test marks returned late or not at all, close to when marks are posted, is useless because students don’t understand the weight of various marks and how they will be reflected overall.
Having a pulse on where students are tracking is imperative. It’s like asking someone to drive a car and not knowing what their gas levels are like. This is only one small part of mental well-being at Del. 
Overall, Del needs to focus on improving student happiness. Students often feel like there’s no fun at Del due to the many restrictions and rules. These limitations are focused on liability, which can be frustrating.
Del has fantastic facilities that many parents have contributed to through donations and fundraisers. However, these facilities are rarely used because of the daily restrictions imposed on students. The requirements to use the facilities, not only during the day but also after school or on weekends, are challenging.
The primary purpose of renting out these facilities is to generate revenue for the school, which is admirable. However, the pace and volume of rentals impact current students who can’t enjoy the facilities their parents helped fund.
Communication is another area that Del needs to improve. Clear, accurate, and consistent communication is imperative. Lengthy emails on Friday evenings at 6 p.m. are not welcome and often go unread. 
Lastly, Del needs to improve its tone and messaging. Last year was a difficult year for Del Staff, students, and parents. The tone and message often communicated by various members of the board and below was insulting and offensive to the parent and staff body. These comments do not align with the Lasallian value of respectful human relationships in the comm.
Del needs to understand that parents have choices about where to place their children and that they don’t simply do this because of low tuition, which we are often reminded of. The respect that is expected of students should be the same respect that the parent community is offered. Parents often feel like they are “in the way,” “too involved,” “too opinionated,” and that their feelings and beliefs don’t matter.
Fostering a relationship in this comm of kindness, respect, admiration, and genuine gratitude would go a long way.

column15:
I appreciate the rigorous education Del tries to offer, focusing on core classics as they pertain to English grammar, writing and literature. Del has several seasoned teachers, and you can be assured of a solid education if your child has the good fortune to be taught by one of them. 

I also like the co-ed environment and the fact that we offer bursaries to students who might otherwise not have them. Additionally, I appreciate the “fun” that the PA community creates for the school. It’s evident that the PA and volunteer community genuinely cares and wants to do their best for all our students. Some parents give a lot of their time to various events like Terry F Day and Del Shoppe, and it often seems like the same group of parents. However, I’m concerned about the future if new parents don’t step up and contribute in the same way. What will this look like for upcoming students?

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15:
In no particular order. 

In no particular order, here are some suggestions for improvement:

- Prioritize mental health: Focus on finding resources and tools to support our students. Dig deep to understand what students face daily, where they struggle, and why. Offer various ways to support all students. As it relates to academics and the impacts marking and assessments have on students, this could mean looking at different testing environments, different ways to assess students and their progress vs just a mark-based system. 

- Retain teachers: Ensure that teachers in the latter grades (11 and 12) are strong in their teaching so that students’ learning is not compromised. Respond swiftly to parent feedback regarding teacher concerns. We shouldn’t wait until the new year or beyond to address recurring issues.

- Provide support to new teachers: Regularly check-in with new teachers in the classroom. Analyze class and cohort averages, and compare them to previous years if a different teacher taught the subject.

- Refocus on treatment of others: Del needs to reconsider its treatment of parents, staff, and students. Truly listen to others, welcome their feedback, and take action. Don’t pretend to solicit feedback only to continue doing the same things over and over. Allow everyone to share their thoughts and opinions without fear of being judged, terminated or penalized in some other way. 

- Present all data of this survey: Regardless of the results, present all the data,  including the good, the bad, and the ugly. Being transparent and addressing the real core issues will be key to the ongoing success and reputation of DLS.

column15:
Several parents have recently expressed a shared concern regarding our graduates’ university placements. It has been observed that a significant number of our students are concentrated in Western University and Queen’s University. While both institutions are reputable in Canada, it is worth noting that in recent years, certain corporations—particularly in the banking and finance sectors—have reduced their recruitment from these universities.

We would like the school to review and assess how well our students are being prepared for competitive college and university applications, both in Canada and the United States. Specifically, we are interested in understanding:

How competitive our students are in comparison to peers from other independent schools.

Whether our current academic and counseling programs adequately support applications to top-tier universities in Canada, the U.S., and internationally.

What strategies or enhancements the school might consider to broaden the range of postsecondary options available to our graduates.

column14: What should De La Salle improve most?
column15:
While parents greatly value the school’s nurturing and caring community, many feel that there is room for meaningful improvement in how the school benchmarks its performance. Specifically, the school should strengthen its efforts to objectively measure and demonstrate its academic strength, teacher competencies, and college placement outcomes.
At present, statements of pride in our accomplishments are not always supported by clear data or comparative evidence. Parents believe it is important for the school to adopt more transparent and data-driven benchmarking—both against national and international academic standards, and against other leading independent schools. This will help ensure that our students are not only well cared for but also well prepared and competitive in their academic and postsecondary pursuits.
